subject: maths
title: Chapter 8 · Test 2
summary: A 15-question test on Year 8 Chapter 8: sampling and bias, comparing data sets, complementary events, Venn diagrams and two-way tables, and experimental probability.
body:
This test covers Chapter 8, Probability and statistics: samples and populations, comparing data sets, probability and complementary events, Venn diagrams and two-way tables, and experimental probability.

## How to do this test

- **Time:** about 25 minutes.
- **Conditions:** no notes and no calculator unless the question says. Show your working on paper.
- **Diagrams:** many questions have a graph, dot plot, spinner, grid or Venn diagram — read the numbers on it carefully.
- **Levels:** 4 easy, 5 medium, 4 hard and 2 challenge questions.
- **After marking:** for each question you got wrong, go back to the lesson it came from and redo its worked examples. Then try another Chapter 8 test — each one has different questions on the same skills.

questions.prompt: To find out how often people in her city go to the beach, Lena surveys 100 people on the sand at a city beach on a hot Sunday. What is the main problem with her sample?

options.A: It is too small: with 1000 people at the beach it would be fair
options.B: It is a census, so it can’t be used to estimate
options.C: There is no problem, because Lena did not choose who was at the beach
options.D: It is biased: people already at the beach probably go more often than most people in the city

questions.explanation: Everyone in the sample is already at the beach, so they are not typical of the whole city — the sample is biased. Making it bigger would not help, because every extra person would also be a beachgoer.
steps: Ask who could be in the sample: only people at the beach on that day.
Those people are more likely than average to go to the beach often, so the sample is biased — whatever its size.

mistakes.A: Step 2: a bigger sample does not fix bias. 1000 beachgoers would still lean the same way.
mistakes.B: Step 1: only 100 people out of a whole city were asked, so it is a sample, not a census.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the place she chose decides who can be in the sample — and only beachgoers can be.

questions.prompt: A suburb has 900 homes. The column graph shows the main type of heating in a random sample of 60 of them. Estimate how many homes in the suburb mainly use electric heating.
questions.explanation: The sample fraction is 21/60 = 0.35, and 0.35 × 900 = 315 homes. Treating 21 as 21% (giving 189) forgets that the sample has 60 homes, not 100.
steps: Read the graph: 21 of the 60 homes in the sample use electric heating.
Fraction of the sample: 21/60 = 0.35. Assume the suburb is the same, because the sample is random.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 21/60 = 35% is the percentage of the sample. Multiply the fraction by all 900 homes.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 21 is a count out of 60, not 21%. Use the fraction 21/60.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 900 − 21 doesn’t estimate anything. Multiply the sample fraction by 900.

questions.diagram_alt: Column graph for a sample of 60 homes: gas 27, electric 21, wood 6, none 6

questions.prompt: The column graph shows the number of workers in each department of a company. A stratified sample of 20 workers is chosen so that each department is in the same proportion as in the company. How many warehouse workers should be in the sample?
questions.explanation: Half of the 240 workers are in the warehouse, so half of the 20-person sample — 10 workers — should come from there. Giving each department about 6.7 places ignores the different department sizes.

mistakes.A: Step 2: sharing the 20 places equally between 3 departments ignores their sizes. Use each department’s fraction of all the workers.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 120/240 = 50% is the percentage of the company. Multiply the fraction by the sample size, 20.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 120 ÷ 20 divides the department by the sample size. Find the department’s fraction of the company (120/240) first.

questions.diagram_alt: Column graph of workers: sales 84, office 36, warehouse 120

questions.prompt: The parallel dot plots show how many texts Ivy and Jo sent on each day of one week. What is the range of Ivy’s data?
questions.explanation: Ivy’s values go from 2 to 12, so her range is 12 − 2 = 10. 12 is just her largest value, not the range.
steps: Read Ivy’s dot plot: the smallest value is 2 and the largest is 12.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 12 is Ivy’s largest value. The range is largest − smallest.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 4 is the range of Jo’s data. Use the top dot plot, Ivy’s.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 5 is Ivy’s median (the middle value). The range is largest − smallest.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel dot plots of texts per day: Ivy has dots at 2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 8 and 12; Jo has dots at 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8 and 9

questions.prompt: The weekly pocket money of seven friends is $10, $12, $12, $15, $16, $18 and $85. Which measure gives the best idea of a typical amount, and what is it?
questions.explanation: Because $85 is an outlier, the median ($15) is the best typical value; the mean ($24) is more than six of the seven amounts. With 7 values the median is the single 4th value, so it is not $15.50.
steps: Notice the outlier: $85 is far from the other amounts.
An outlier drags the mean, so use the median.
Seven values in order, so the median is the 4th: $15.

mistakes.A: Step 1: $85 is an outlier and drags the mean up — six of the seven friends get less than $24. Use the median.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the range measures spread, not a typical value. Use a measure of centre.
mistakes.C: Step 3: with 7 values there is one middle value (the 4th). Only average two middle values when there is an even number of values.

questions.prompt: In a maths test, the 24 students in Class A had a mean of 70 and the 16 students in Class B had a mean of 80. What is the mean for all 40 students?
questions.explanation: The totals are 1680 and 1280, so the overall mean is 2960 ÷ 40 = 74. Averaging the two means (75) ignores that Class A has more students.

mistakes.A: Step 3: (70 + 80) ÷ 2 treats the classes as the same size. Find each class’s total first.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 70 + 80 adds the two means. Add the class totals and divide by 40.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you matched the sizes to the wrong means. Class A (24 students) has mean 70: 24 × 70.

questions.prompt: The bag in the diagram holds 5 blue counters and 7 white counters. One counter is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is NOT blue?
questions.explanation: P(blue) = 5/12, so P(not blue) = 1 − 5/12 = 7/12 (the 7 white counters out of 12). 5/12 is the chance of blue, not of “not blue”.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 5/12 is the probability that it IS blue. Subtract it from 1.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 5/7 compares blue with white. A probability compares with ALL 12 counters.
mistakes.D: Step 2: a probability can never be more than 1. Work out 1 − 5/12.

questions.diagram_alt: A bag of 12 counters: 5 blue (B) and 7 white (W)

questions.prompt: A fair spinner has 10 equal sections numbered 1 to 10. What is the probability of spinning a number that is at least 3?
questions.explanation: The complement of “at least 3” is spinning 1 or 2, which has probability 2/10, so the answer is 1 − 2/10 = 8/10 = 4/5. 7/10 forgets that 3 itself counts as “at least 3”.
steps: The complement of “at least 3” is “less than 3”: just 1 and 2.

mistakes.A: Step 1: “at least 3” includes 3 itself. The complement is only 1 and 2.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 2/10 = 1/5 is the probability of 1 or 2 (the complement). Subtract it from 1.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 1, 2 and 3 are not the complement — 3 belongs to “at least 3”. The complement is only 1 and 2.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the two numbers are multiplied. The grid shows every product. What is the probability that the product is less than 30?
questions.explanation: Only 3 of the 36 cells (30, 30 and 36) are 30 or more, so P(less than 30) = 1 − 3/36 = 11/12. 17/18 misses that 30 appears in two cells.
steps: There are 36 equally likely cells. The complement of “less than 30” is “30 or more”.
Products of 30 or more: 30 (two cells) and 36 (one cell) — 3 cells, so P = 3/36 = 1/12.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 3/36 = 1/12 is the probability of a product of 30 or more. Subtract it from 1.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 30 appears twice in the grid (5 × 6 and 6 × 5). Count every cell, so there are 3 cells of 30 or more.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the numbers 1 to 29 are not the outcomes. Count the 36 cells in the grid.

questions.diagram_alt: A 6 by 6 grid showing the product of two dice for each of the 36 outcomes, from 1 to 36

questions.prompt: The Venn diagram shows which of 25 students play soccer and which go swimming. How many students go swimming but do NOT play soccer?
questions.explanation: The part of the Swimming circle outside the Soccer circle holds 9 students. 14 also counts the 5 students in the overlap, who do play soccer.
steps: “Swimming but not soccer” means inside the Swimming circle but outside the Soccer circle.
That is the “swimming only” region, which holds 9 students.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 9 + 5 is the whole Swimming circle. The 5 in the overlap also play soccer, so leave them out.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 5 is the overlap — those students swim AND play soccer.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 4 is outside both circles, so those students do neither.

questions.diagram_alt: Venn diagram for 25 students: soccer only 7, both soccer and swimming 5, swimming only 9, neither 4

questions.prompt: A number is chosen at random from 1 to 20. A is the event “a multiple of 4” and B is the event “a multiple of 6”. What is P(A and B)?
questions.explanation: Only 12 is a multiple of both 4 and 6, so P(A and B) = 1/20. 7/20 is P(A or B), which counts everything in either list.
steps: A and B means in both lists: only 12.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 7/20 is P(A or B) — everything in either circle. “And” is only the overlap.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 5 + 3 = 8 adds the two lists and counts 12 twice. “And” means numbers in BOTH lists.
mistakes.D: Step 2: a number can be in both lists without being a multiple of 4 × 6 = 24. Look for numbers in both lists, like 12.

questions.prompt: At a concert there are 120 people: 70 adults and 50 children. Altogether 45 people bought a T-shirt, and 15 of these were children. One person is chosen at random. What is the probability that the person is an adult who did NOT buy a T-shirt?
questions.explanation: 30 adults bought a T-shirt, so 40 adults did not, and P = 40/120 = 1/3. 4/7 would be right only if the person were chosen from the adults alone.

mistakes.A: Step 3: the person is chosen from everyone (120), not just from the adults. Divide by 120.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 70 − 45 takes away the children’s T-shirts too. Only 45 − 15 = 30 adults bought one.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 75 is everyone without a T-shirt, children included. You want adults without one.

questions.prompt: A spinner with 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5 was spun 250 times. The column graph shows the results. What is the experimental probability of spinning an even number?
questions.explanation: Even means 2 or 4, which came up 52 + 55 = 107 times out of 250, so the experimental probability is 0.428. 0.4 is the theory, not what the experiment gave.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 2/5 = 0.4 is the theoretical probability. The question asks for the experimental probability from the results.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 46 + 49 + 48 = 143 are the ODD results. Even means 2 or 4.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 52 is only the number of 2s. Even means 2 or 4, so add both bars.

questions.diagram_alt: Column graph of 250 spins: 1 came up 46 times, 2 came up 52, 3 came up 49, 4 came up 55 and 5 came up 48

questions.prompt: A bag holds 20 marbles, some green and the rest yellow. Kai draws a marble, records its colour and puts it back. He does this 150 times and gets green 52 times. What is the best estimate of the number of green marbles in the bag?
questions.explanation: Green came up 52 times in 150 draws, so about 0.347 of the marbles are green: 0.347 × 20 ≈ 6.9, which rounds to 7. Writing 6 cuts off the decimal instead of rounding.
steps: About 0.347 of the 20 marbles are green: 0.347 × 20 ≈ 6.9.
Marbles are whole, so the best estimate is 7 green marbles.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 6.93 is much closer to 7 than to 6 — round to the nearest whole number, don’t cut off the decimal.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 150 ÷ 52 is upside down. Experimental probability = successes ÷ trials = 52 ÷ 150.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 52 is the number of green draws, not marbles — there are only 20 marbles. Use the fraction 52/150.

questions.prompt: Scientists catch 60 birds on an island, put a band on each leg and release them. A month later they catch 45 birds, and 9 of these have bands (shown in the diagram). Estimate the number of birds on the island.
questions.explanation: In the second catch 9/45 = 1/5 have bands, so the 60 banded birds are about 1/5 of the island’s birds: 60 × 5 = 300. 12 comes from turning the fraction upside down.
steps: Fraction banded in the second catch: 9/45 = 1/5.
Assume 1/5 of all the birds are banded, so the 60 banded birds are 1/5 of the total.

mistakes.A: Step 1: adding 60 + 45 + 9 doesn’t use the idea of a sample. Use the fraction banded in the second catch.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 60 × 9 ÷ 45 has the fraction upside down. The 60 banded birds are 9/45 of ALL the birds, so divide 60 by 9/45.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 60 + 45 − 9 counts the birds caught, not the birds on the island. Use the fraction banded in the second catch.

questions.diagram_alt: The second catch of 45 birds drawn as 45 dots, with the 9 banded birds shaded
